sub_strands.sub_strand: Pronunciation and Listening (Theme 1: Child labour)
learning_experiences: listen to an oral narrative from a digital device or a text read by the teacher,
listen for specific information such as sounds: /ɪə/ as in tear, appear, rear, clear and severe from a text,
listen for the main idea from a text and practise saying words with the sound /ɪə/,
infer the meaning of vocabulary and phrases using contextual clues, answer oral questions based on listening comprehension,
use digital and print resources to look up the meaning and spelling of words,
retell a story and record the narration on a digital device,

use expressions such as fixed phrases: play games, far away, believe it or not, do your best, burst into tears; similes: as hungry as a wolf, as greedy as a hyena; metaphors: The thief was a hyena, he was so greedy; idioms: work like a dog, dog tired, work for peanuts, donkey work; proverbs: all work and no play makes Jack a dull boy, phrasal verbs: beat up, agree with, put up with, cope with.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should you listen keenly?
Why should you pronounce words accurately?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Digital Literacy: The learner manipulates digital devices when listening to an oral narrative.
Learning to Learn: The learner carries out activities with peers as they practise pronunciation of words.
sub_strands.values:
Respect: The learner interacts with information on equity as they listen to texts related to child labour.
Responsibility: The learner shows accountability when listening to an oral narrative from a digital device.
sub_strands.pcis: Child Rights: This is addressed as the learner interacts with texts on child labour.
sub_strands.links: Vocabulary learnt on the theme of child labour can be applied to the learning of child rights in Social Studies.

outcomes.text: select words with the target sound /ɪə/ from an oral narrative
use vocabulary related to the theme in sentences correctly
use proverbs, fixed phrases, idioms, and metaphors with straightforward meanings in oral communication
listen for the main idea and specific details from an oral text
value the importance of listening attentively

skills.name: Know idioms and fixed phrases
skills.mastery: Gives the meaning of idioms and fixed phrases (work like a dog, dog tired, burst into tears, a piece of cake, under the weather), completes them with the right word, and does not read them word for word, in 8 of 10 new items.

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use words about child labour and child rights
skills.mastery: Chooses the right word from the theme (employ, exploit, labour, wages, trafficking, abuse, rescue, protect) to complete a sentence, and does not mix a person with an action, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Find the main idea and specific details of a text
skills.mastery: Chooses the sentence or title that covers the whole text, tells it from a detail, and finds a specific detail asked for, in 8 of 10 new texts.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Reads an idiom word for word.

example.question: What does "dog tired" mean?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "tired like a dog" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An idiom's meaning is not the sum of its words.
misconceptions.feedback: An idiom means something different from its words. Dog tired means extremely tired.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Changes a word of the idiom (work like a cat).

example.question: He had to work like a ___ all day.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "cat" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An idiom is fixed. Change one word and it is lost.
misconceptions.feedback: An idiom is a fixed phrase. You cannot change its words: work like a dog.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Takes the opposite meaning of an idiom.

example.question: What does "a piece of cake" mean?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "very difficult" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Ask what the picture suggests: cake is easy to eat.
misconceptions.feedback: A piece of cake means very easy.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses an idiom in a situation it does not fit.

example.question: When would you say "burst into tears"?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "when you are very happy" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Match the idiom to the feeling or the event.
misconceptions.feedback: Burst into tears means to begin to cry suddenly.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a word for the person where the action is needed (employer for employ).

example.question: It is against the law to ___ young children to work.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "employer" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Employ is the action. The employer is the person who does it.
misconceptions.feedback: An employer is a person. Employ is the action. Choose the word for the action here.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Takes a harsh word for a kind one (exploit for protect).

example.question: The law is there to ___ children from harm.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "exploit" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Exploit means to use someone unfairly. Protect means to keep safe.
misconceptions.feedback: To exploit is to use someone unfairly. To protect is to keep them safe.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes wages (pay for work) with fees (pay for a service).

example.question: The boy was paid very low ___ for a full day of hard work.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "fees" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Wages: money paid for work. Fees: money you pay for school or a service.
misconceptions.feedback: Wages are money paid for work. Fees are money you pay for school or a service.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a detail as the main idea.

example.question: What is the main idea?
example.correct_answer: what the whole passage is about

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a detail" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The main idea covers all of the passage.
misconceptions.feedback: The main idea covers the whole text. A detail is only one part.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks an idea that is wider than the passage.

example.question: What is the main idea?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a very general statement" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The main idea fits this passage, not every passage.
misconceptions.feedback: The main idea must fit this passage. A very general statement is too wide.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks an idea that is not in the passage.

example.question: What is the main idea?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "something not in the text" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Check the idea against the text.
misconceptions.feedback: The main idea must be in the passage. Check each answer against it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives the main idea when a specific detail is asked, or the reverse.

example.question: What time did the bus leave?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "it left late" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A detail question asks for one fact, like a time or a name.
misconceptions.feedback: A specific detail question wants the exact fact, such as a time, name or place.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Extensive Reading (Theme 1: Child labour)
learning_experiences: select age-appropriate reference materials from print and non-print sources,
read selected reference materials independently,
search for information on child labour from reference materials,
compile a list of new words and their meaning,
create a crossword puzzle from the list of new words,
make notes on the information they have obtained.
key_inquiry_questions: How do you select the books you read?
Why do you read books?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Digital Literacy: The learner uses digital technology as they select age-appropriate reference materials from digital sources.
Communication and Collaboration: The learner recognises the values of others’ ideas when selecting appropriate reading materials in collaboration with peers.
sub_strands.values:
Unity. The learner displays team spirit while obtaining information about child labour and shares it with peers.
Respect: The learner appreciates diverse opinions as they collaborate in material selection.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the skills acquired in listening comprehension to the acquisition of listening skills in Kiswahili.
sub_strands.design_notes: Second read left this for a person to confirm: pcis: not in the design.

outcomes.text: select appropriate reading materials in collaboration with peers
read a variety of materials independently for information and pleasure
use reference materials to find the required information
judge the suitability of sample extensive reading materials

skills.name: Use reference materials: dictionary, atlas, index and contents
skills.mastery: Chooses the right reference for a need, puts words in alphabetical order beyond the first letter, and decides from guide words whether a word is on a page, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Judge whether a book or text suits a purpose
skills.mastery: Chooses the book or text that fits a reader's purpose, level and interest (information, enjoyment, a topic), and does not choose by the cover, the length or the title alone, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: choose the book for a purpose
judge the relevance of a text

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Chooses the wrong reference book.

example.question: Which book helps you find a country on the map?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "dictionary" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Dictionary: words. Atlas: maps. Encyclopaedia: facts.
misconceptions.feedback: A dictionary gives word meanings, an atlas has maps, an encyclopaedia gives facts on many topics.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Orders words by first letter only.

example.question: Put in alphabetical order: bread, brave, brick.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "bread, brave, brick" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: When the first letters match, look at the next letter.
misconceptions.feedback: When the first letters are the same, look at the second, third and so on.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Misreads guide words.

example.question: Guide words are "farm" and "feast". Which word is on the page?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "fence" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The word must come after the first guide and before the last.
misconceptions.feedback: A word is on the page only if it falls between the two guide words in alphabetical order.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the contents page when the index is needed or the reverse.

example.question: Which part of a book lists the page for one small topic?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "contents" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Contents: chapters in order. Index: every topic in A to Z.
misconceptions.feedback: The contents lists the chapters in order. The index lists small topics A to Z with page numbers.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a story to find facts or a fact book for enjoyment.

example.question: Which book would help you learn how bees make honey?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a story about a bee" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Information: facts. Story: enjoyment.
misconceptions.feedback: Use an information book to learn facts. A story is for enjoyment.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Judges a book by its cover or its size.

example.question: What is the best way to judge if a book suits you?
example.correct_answer: read the blurb and a page

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "look at the cover only" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The blurb and a page show the topic and the level.
misconceptions.feedback: The cover can mislead. Read the blurb and a page to see the topic and the level.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a text far too hard or far too easy.

example.question: Which text is right for a learner in Grade 6?
example.wrong_answer: a text with many unknown words on every line
example.correct_answer: a text with a few new words

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a text with many unknown words on every line" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A good book has a few new words, not every line.
misconceptions.feedback: A text is right if you understand most of it and meet only a few new words.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a text on a different topic.

example.question: Which text is relevant for a project on Lake Victoria?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a text about the desert" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Check the topic first.
misconceptions.feedback: A relevant text is about the same topic as your need.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Word Classes (Theme 1: Child labour)
content_topics: Determiners - some, enough, each, and a lot of
learning_experiences: identify the determiners some, enough, each and a lot of in sentences,
complete online quizzes and exercises involving the use of some, enough, each, and a lot of,
construct sentences using determiners,
make sentences using determiners from substitution tables,
correct the sentences constructed by a peer,
work in groups and determine the correctness of a sample of sentences.
key_inquiry_questions: How do we express the quantity or amount of something?
Why should we give the exact amount of something?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication and Collaboration: The learner contributes to group decision making when identifying sentences featuring determiners from a print or digital text.
Digital Literacy: The learner interacts with technology when completing online quizzes and exercises involving the use of determiners.
sub_strands.values: Social justice: The learner fosters fairness by reviewing the sentences constructed by a peer. Responsibility: The learner engages in assigned roles as they construct sentences using determiners.
sub_strands.pcis: Peace Education: The learner nurtures social cohesion as they work in groups to determine the correctness of a sample of sentences.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the concept of determiners when editing their written work in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify determiners some, enough, each, and a lot of, in texts
use determiners some, enough, each, and a lot of, in sentences correctly
collaborate with peers to judge the correct use of determiners in sentences

skills.name: Use some, enough, each and a lot of
skills.mastery: Chooses some, enough, each or a lot of to fit the noun and the verb (each takes a singular noun and verb, a lot of takes plural or uncountable, some in an offer or a statement), and does not write each of the boys are or a lots of, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses each with a plural noun or a plural verb.

example.question: Each of the girls ___ a bottle.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "have" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Each means one at a time: one girl, one bottle, so the verb is singular.
misconceptions.feedback: Each points to one person or thing at a time, so the verb is singular: each girl has.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes a lots of or a lot off.

example.question: We saw ___ goats at the market.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a lots of" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Say the whole phrase: a lot of. Lots of has no a in front.
misconceptions.feedback: The phrase is a lot of (one lot) or lots of. A lots of is not used.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts enough in the wrong place (enough big, instead of big enough).

example.question: The room is ___ for all of us.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "enough big" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After an adjective, enough comes last: big enough. Before a noun it comes first: enough chairs.
misconceptions.feedback: Enough comes AFTER an adjective (big enough) and BEFORE a noun (enough chairs).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses some where a question or a refusal needs any, or any in a plain statement.

example.question: There is not ___ milk left.

misconceptions.cause: Learns that some means a few and uses it in every sentence.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "some" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Some is for plain statements and offers. In a negative sentence use any.
misconceptions.feedback: In a sentence with not, use any, not some: There is not any milk.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Guided Writing (Theme 1: Child labour)
learning_experiences: discuss different types of forms they have filled in groups,
work jointly to search for relevant sample forms from the internet,
download relevant forms and fill them,
fill in the basic details, personal information, and the why details in a form,
design a form with basic, personal, and why details in small groups.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do we fill forms?
Why is it important to fill forms accurately and correctly?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and Imagination: The learner gains new perspectives on how to undertake a task as they design forms.
Digital Literacy: The learner manipulates digital devices as they search, download, and fill in the relevant information in forms.
sub_strands.values: Social Justice: The learner fosters fairness by according equal opportunities to peers when searching for relevant sample forms from the internet.
sub_strands.pcis: Social cohesion: The learner nurtures social cohesion as they design a form with basic, personal, and why details in small groups.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the concept of filling forms to the learning of the same concept in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: record specific details on forms to convey information
design a form to provide the required information
advocate the importance of filling forms correctly

skills.name: Fill in and plan a form
skills.mastery: Puts each detail in the field it belongs to (surname, date of birth, signature), follows the form's own instruction (block letters, tick one, write N/A), and says which fields a form needs for its purpose, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: choose the entry for a field
choose the field a form needs

misconceptions.error: Puts the first name in the surname space or the other way round.

example.question: Wanjiru Kamau Mwangi is filling in a form. Her surname is Mwangi. What goes in the box "Surname"?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Wanjiru" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The surname is the family name, the name shared with the family.
misconceptions.feedback: The surname is the family name. The form asks for it in its own box, apart from the first name.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes today's date in the date of birth box.

example.question: Which goes in the box "Date of birth"?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the date today" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Date of birth is the day you were born.
misconceptions.feedback: Date of birth is the day you were born, not the day you fill in the form.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves a box empty instead of writing N/A or none.

example.question: The box "Allergies" does not apply to Peter. What should he write?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "leave it empty" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An empty box looks as if you forgot. Write none or N/A.
misconceptions.feedback: Do not leave a box empty. If it does not apply, write N/A or none so the reader knows you saw it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes in small letters when the form asks for block letters.

example.question: The form says "Write in BLOCK LETTERS". Which way is right?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "amina odhiambo" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Block letters are all capital letters.
misconceptions.feedback: Block letters are capital letters, printed clearly, so every box can be read.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Plans a form with a field that has nothing to do with its purpose, or leaves out the one it needs.

example.question: A school wants someone to call in an emergency. Which field must the form have?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Favourite colour" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Ask: what will the reader do with this information? Keep only what the purpose needs.
misconceptions.feedback: A form asks only for what its purpose needs. Think about what the reader will do with each answer.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Prints the name in the signature space.

example.question: What do you put in the box "Signature"?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "your name in print" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A signature is your own handwriting of your name.
misconceptions.feedback: A signature is your name written in your own style, by hand, not printed.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Pronunciation and Listening Comprehension (Theme 2: Cultural and religious celebrations)
learning_experiences: listen to a comprehension passage of about 150 words,
pronounce words containing the sounds /l/ and /r/,
say tongue twisters with the target sounds after the teacher,
work jointly to give the meaning of new words and use them in sentences,

use expressions correctly, for example, - metaphor: Peter is a giraffe- he is so tall. - idiom: a red letter day, kill two birds with one stone, feel at home - proverbs: charity begins at home, - phrasal verb: pass by, look forward to, look for, look at, - use the expressions to create a paragraph.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should you pronounce words correctly?
Why do we use proverbs?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Self-efficacy: The learner expresses themselves clearly as they practise pronouncing words containing the sounds /l/ and /r/.
Creativity and Imagination: The learner undertakes group tasks as they use proverbs to create a paragraph in pairs or groups.
sub_strands.values: Unity is enhanced as the learner works jointly with peers to give the meaning of new words and use them in sentence
sub_strands.pcis: Cultural awareness: this is enhanced as the learner interacts with common sayings and expressions from different cultures.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to link the concept of usinf expressions to their learning in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify proverbs from a text for effective communication
listen for the main idea and specific details from a text
use words and expressions such as similes, metaphors and proverbs containing selected sounds correctly
value the importance of attentive listening in communication

skills.name: Know proverbs and use them
skills.mastery: Matches a proverb to its meaning, finishes it with the right word and picks the situation it fits, and does not read it word for word, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Tell similes from metaphors and complete them
skills.mastery: Says that a simile compares with like or as and a metaphor says one thing is another, completes familiar similes (as hungry as a wolf), and does not write as ... like, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Reads a proverb word for word.

example.question: What does "A stitch in time saves nine" mean?
example.correct_answer: Fix a small problem early so it does not grow.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Sewing is useful." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A proverb gives advice by a picture. Ask: what is the lesson?
misconceptions.feedback: A proverb uses a picture to teach a lesson. Read what it teaches, not the words one by one.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Takes the opposite lesson from a proverb.

example.question: What does "Haste makes waste" mean?
example.wrong_answer: Hurry and you will get more done.
example.correct_answer: Hurrying leads to mistakes and loss.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Hurry and you will get more done." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Waste is a bad result: the proverb warns.
misconceptions.feedback: Haste makes waste warns that hurrying spoils the work.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes two proverbs of a similar kind.

example.question: Which proverb tells us to keep what we already have?
example.wrong_answer: Too many cooks spoil the broth.
example.correct_answer: A bird in the hand is worth two in the bush.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Too many cooks spoil the broth." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Match the lesson of each proverb, not only one word.
misconceptions.feedback: Each proverb has its own lesson. A bird in the hand is about keeping what you have.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Finishes a proverb with the wrong word.

example.question: Where there is a will, there is a ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "door" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Proverbs are fixed. Say it in full to remember it.
misconceptions.feedback: A proverb is fixed. It cannot be changed: Where there is a will, there is a way.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Calls a metaphor a simile.

example.question: Which sentence has a metaphor?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "He ran like the wind." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A simile uses like or as. A metaphor says one thing IS another.
misconceptions.feedback: A simile compares with like or as. A metaphor says one thing is another, with no like or as.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes as ... like instead of as ... as.

example.question: He was as hungry ___ a wolf.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "like" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The pattern is as ... as, or just like.
misconceptions.feedback: A simile uses as ... as (as hungry as) or like by itself. Do not write as hungry like.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong animal or thing in a familiar simile.

example.question: As greedy as a ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "giraffe" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Similes are fixed: greedy as a hyena, brave as a lion.
misconceptions.feedback: Common similes are fixed. Greedy goes with hyena, brave with lion.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Calls a plain statement a simile.

example.question: Which sentence has a simile?
example.correct_answer: My dog is as big as a calf.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "My dog is big." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A simile compares two different things.
misconceptions.feedback: A simile compares two different things using like or as. A plain statement does not compare.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Intensive Reading (Theme 2: Cultural and religious celebrations)
learning_experiences: read a poem or story and identify the characters and events,
read a story of about 500 words and predict the events,
answer factual and inferential questions,
collaborate with peers to recite a poem,
summarise events in a story by retelling it in small groups,
create crossword puzzles using learnt vocabulary,
collaborate with peers to describe characters or places in poems or stories.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do we enjoy reading stories and poems?
Which stories and poems have you read?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication and Collaboration: The learner recognises the value of others’ opinions as they work with peers to describe characters or events in poems and stories.
Creativity and Imagination: The learner undertakes tasks that encourage artistic expression of ideas while creating crossword puzzles using learnt vocabulary.
sub_strands.values:
Respect: The learner respects the opinion of others as they collaborate with peers to recite a poem.
Love: The learner shows a caring attitude as they collaborate with peers to describe characters or places in poems or stories.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skills: Effective communication is enhanced as the learner becomes more proficient in reading.
sub_strands.links: The skill of predicting events in a story is relevant to the concept of storytelling in Religious Education.

outcomes.text: identify characters and events in a text for comprehension
predict events in a text accurately
answer factual and inferential questions correctly for comprehension
create mental images from the events in poems and stories
judge the characters or events in a story in collaboration with peers

skills.name: Name characters, places and events and put events in order
skills.mastery: Names the characters and the places in a short story, and puts four of its events in the order they happened, in 8 of 10 new passages.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Predict what happens next
skills.mastery: Uses clues in the story to choose the most likely next event and says which clue supports it, in 8 of 10 new passages.
question_forms: choose the clue that supports it

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Answer factual questions from a text
skills.mastery: Finds an answer that is stated in the text, tells true from false and not stated, and does not pick a detail that sits near the answer, in 8 of 10 new passages.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Answer inferential questions from a text
skills.mastery: Works out what the text does not say outright (why a character acts, how they feel) and does not give an answer the text contradicts or merely repeats, in 8 of 10 new passages.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Create mental images from a poem or story
skills.mastery: Picks the words of a poem or story that make a picture, and says what the writer wants the reader to see, hear or feel, and does not pick the line that only gives a fact, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: choose the line that paints a picture

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Judge a character from what they say and do
skills.mastery: Chooses the trait that the character's words and actions support (kind, selfish, brave, honest), and says which line is the evidence, and does not judge from the name or one word, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Names a minor character for the main one.

example.question: Who is the story mostly about?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the shopkeeper" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The main character is in most of the events.
misconceptions.feedback: The main character is the one most of the story is about.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Names the wrong place.

example.question: Where did the story happen?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "at the bus stop" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Find the sentence that tells where.
misconceptions.feedback: The place is where the events happen. Read the first lines again.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Reverses the order of events.

example.question: Put the events in order.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "D, C, B, A" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Find the event that happens first.
misconceptions.feedback: Find the first event, then the next, using words such as then and after.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Swaps two events that are next to each other.

example.question: Put the events in order.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "A, C, B, D" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Check each pair: which happened first?
misconceptions.feedback: Check each pair of events. Words like before and after show which came first.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives a place when a character is asked, or the other way round.

example.question: Who helped the boy?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the village" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A character is a person or animal; a place is where.
misconceptions.feedback: A character is a person or animal that acts. A place is where the story happens.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Predicts something with no clue in the passage.

example.question: What will probably happen next?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a lion will arrive" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A prediction needs a clue from the passage.
misconceptions.feedback: A good prediction follows from a clue in the passage.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Predicts something that goes against the passage.

example.question: What will probably happen next?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "she will give up" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The prediction must agree with what the passage shows about the character.
misconceptions.feedback: A prediction must agree with the clues. This one goes against them.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives something that has already happened as a prediction.

example.question: What will probably happen next?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "she carried the bag" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A prediction is about what comes after the passage.
misconceptions.feedback: A prediction is about what happens next, not what was already told.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a detail that is close to the answer but is not the answer.

example.question: What did she carry?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a basket" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Read the exact sentence the question points to.
misconceptions.feedback: Read the exact sentence the question points to. A detail nearby is not always the answer.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Answers from what he or she knows, not from the passage.

example.question: What did they use to make it?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "grass" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The answer is in the passage.
misconceptions.feedback: The answer must come from the passage, not from what you already know.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says the passage does not say something that it does say.

example.question: Is it true, false or not stated?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Not stated" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Search the passage again for the sentence.
misconceptions.feedback: Look again. The passage does say it, in the sentence on that point.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says true when the passage says something different.

example.question: Is it true, false or not stated?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "True" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Compare your statement with the sentence in the passage word by word.
misconceptions.feedback: The passage says something different, so the statement is false.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says not stated when the passage says the opposite.

example.question: Is it true, false or not stated?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Not stated" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: If the passage says the opposite, the statement is false.
misconceptions.feedback: The passage does say something about this, and it is different, so the statement is false.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Says true for something that sounds likely but is not written.

example.question: Is it true, false or not stated?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "True" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Find the line. If you cannot, it is not stated.
misconceptions.feedback: If you cannot find the line, it is not stated, even if it sounds likely.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives an answer that the passage goes against.

example.question: Why did she smile?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "She was angry." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Check each answer against the passage.
misconceptions.feedback: An answer must agree with the passage. This one goes against it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives an answer that goes too far beyond the clues.

example.question: What can you tell about her?
example.wrong_answer: She is the richest woman in town.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "She is the richest woman in town." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Stay with what the clues show.
misconceptions.feedback: An inference must stay close to the clues. This one goes too far.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Copies a sentence from the passage as the inference.

example.question: Why did he feel sad?
example.correct_answer: He loved the game and could not play.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The ball burst." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An inference explains; it does not repeat.
misconceptions.feedback: An inference says why. Copying a sentence only repeats what the passage said.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses the line that only gives a fact, not the one that paints a picture.

example.question: Which line paints the clearest picture?
example.correct_answer: Heaps of red tomatoes glowed in the early sun.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The market opens at six." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Look for colours, sounds and movement.
misconceptions.feedback: A line that paints a picture uses colours, sounds, smells or movement, not only a fact.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a picture the words do not show.

example.question: What picture does the poet want you to see?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a quiet night" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Read the key words again: what do they show?
misconceptions.feedback: The words of the poem show the picture. Check each answer against the words.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a picture from one word, ignoring the rest.

example.question: What picture does the poet want you to see?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a river" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Use all the words, not one word.
misconceptions.feedback: Use all the words in the line together to see the picture.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Judges a character from one word or the name.

example.question: Which word best describes her?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "selfish" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Look at what she does and says.
misconceptions.feedback: What a character says and does shows what they are like.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses the opposite trait.

example.question: Which word best describes him?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "lazy" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Check the actions: do they show effort or none?
misconceptions.feedback: The actions in the story show the trait. This trait is the opposite.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks a line that does not show the trait as evidence.

example.question: Which line shows that she is kind?
example.correct_answer: She gave her lunch to a hungry boy.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "She lived in a village." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Evidence is what the character does or says.
misconceptions.feedback: Evidence for a trait is something the character does or says that shows it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Word Classes (Theme 2: Cultural and religious celebrations)
learning_experiences: listen to a story, conversation or poem containing abstract nouns and concrete nouns,
collaborate to pick out concrete and abstract nouns from a story, conversation or poem,
work with peers to construct sentences using concrete and abstract nouns,
make sentences from a substitution table featuring concrete and abstract nouns,
use a laptop, tablet, computer, manila paper, notebook, among others and create a crossword puzzle or a word search, with peers,
share the puzzle or word search through, email, other social media platforms, posters or the school notice board.
key_inquiry_questions: Which things can you see and touch in the classroom?
Which things cannot be seen or touched?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication and Collaboration: The learner recognises the value of others’ views as they make sentences using nouns.
Digital Literacy: The learner interacts with digital devices to create a crossword puzzle or a word search in pairs or groups.
sub_strands.values:
Love: The learner portrays a caring attitude as they collaborate to pick out concrete and abstract nouns from a story, conversation or poem.
Peace: The learner appreciates the importance of peers as they create a crossword puzzle or a word search.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skills: Effective communication is enhanced as the learner practises using nouns in communication.
sub_strands.links: The skill of correct use of concrete and abstract nouns in a variety of contexts relates to the learning of nouns in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify concrete and abstract nouns from a text
use concrete and abstract nouns correctly in a variety of contexts
appreciate the role of concrete and abstract nouns in communication

skills.name: Tell concrete and abstract nouns apart and use them
skills.mastery: Names nouns we can see or touch as concrete (mango, river) and nouns for ideas, feelings and qualities as abstract (honesty, hunger, bravery), and writes the noun form (honesty, not honest) in a gap, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Thinks a feeling or an idea is concrete because it is real.

example.question: Which noun is abstract: river, kindness, table, dog.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "river" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Ask: can I touch it, see it or hear it? Kindness is only in our minds.
misconceptions.feedback: A concrete noun is something you can see or touch. Kindness, fear and freedom are ideas, so they are abstract.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks a place or a group is abstract.

example.question: Which noun is concrete: freedom, market, honesty, courage.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "freedom" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A market is a place you can walk to, so it is concrete.
misconceptions.feedback: Places, people, animals and things are concrete nouns because we can see or touch them.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the adjective where the abstract noun is needed (honest for honesty).

example.question: The headteacher praised her ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "honest" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After her, a noun is needed. The noun for honest is honesty.
misconceptions.feedback: After her or his, a noun is needed. The noun for the quality honest is honesty.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks a sound, a smell or a time word is concrete.

example.question: Which noun is abstract: bell, music, drum, radio.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "bell" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: You can hear music but you cannot hold it; the bell and radio are things.
misconceptions.feedback: Things you can hold are concrete. Things like music, time and hunger cannot be held, so they are abstract.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Creative Writing (Theme 2: Cultural and religious celebrations)
learning_experiences: list topics and possible ideas for open-ended compositions,
discuss in groups ideas and experiences on a given topic,
write down points to guide them in the writing of an open-ended composition on cultural and religious celebrations of about 160-200 words,
collaborate to create the first paragraph,
use expressions, proverbs, idioms fixed phrases, similes and metaphors appropriately in a composition,
complete the composition individually,
Proofread the composition and make necessary corrections,

work with peers to critique an open-ended composition while focusing on: - organisation of ideas (coherence) - creativity - relevance of topic - accuracy of language - (grammar, choice of words, spelling)
grade a composition written by peers.
key_inquiry_questions: How can you make your composition interesting to read?
Why is it important to proofread your composition?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Creativity and Imagination: The learner organises ideas as they create compositions based on a variety of themes.
Learning to Learn: The learner carries out activities with peers as they brainstorm, research and list topics and possible ideas for open-ended compositions in pairs or groups.
sub_strands.values:
Social Justice: The learner fosters inclusivity and non-discrimination as they grade a composition written by peers.
Integrity: The learner follows laid-down procedures when grading peer ́s composition.
sub_strands.pcis: Cultural Awareness: The learner interacts with information on culture as they plan and write an open-ended composition on cultural and religious celebrations.
sub_strands.links: The skills acquired in composition writing are relevant to the writing of essays in Social Studies.

outcomes.text: identify topics and possible ideas for open-ended compositions
organise ideas in a paragraph logically
create an open-ended composition on a variety of themes
judge a narrative composition for correctness of language and relevance of topic

skills.name: Build a paragraph: topic sentence, order and the sentence that does not belong
skills.mastery: Chooses the sentence that opens a paragraph, puts supporting sentences in a logical order and finds the sentence that does not belong, in 8 of 10 new paragraphs.
question_forms: find the sentence that does not belong

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Opens a paragraph with a small detail instead of the main idea.

example.question: Which sentence is the best topic sentence?
example.correct_answer: Our school trip to Nakuru taught us many things.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The bus was blue." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The topic sentence tells what the whole paragraph is about.
misconceptions.feedback: The topic sentence gives the main idea. Details come after it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Keeps a sentence that does not belong to the paragraph's idea.

example.question: Which sentence does not belong in the paragraph?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the sentence about football" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Check each sentence: does it help the main idea?
misconceptions.feedback: Every sentence must help the main idea. A sentence about something else does not belong.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the sentences in the order they come to mind, not the logical order.

example.question: Put these sentences in order.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "C, A, B, D" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Look for first, next, then, finally and for the sentence that sums up.
misconceptions.feedback: Look for time words (first, then, finally) and for an ending sentence. The order should follow what happened.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Ends with a new idea instead of a closing sentence.

example.question: Which sentence best ends the paragraph?
example.wrong_answer: Next week we start a new project.
example.correct_answer: So the trip was a day we will remember.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Next week we start a new project." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The last sentence sums up the paragraph; it does not open a new topic.
misconceptions.feedback: The closing sentence wraps up the paragraph. A new topic belongs in a new paragraph.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Pronunciation and Vocabulary (Theme 3: Etiquette - telephone)
learning_experiences: say words containing the sounds /æ/ and /ɜː/,
assess your peers as they pronounce words with the target sound,
identify polite words and phrases used in a telephone conversation,
role-play a telephone conversation, with peers,
work with peers to use polite language to interrupt politely in sentences,

practise using expressions such as: - fixed phrase: make friends, - simile: as proud as a peacock - metaphor: Peter is a giraffe; he is so tall - idiom: feel at home - proverbs: charity begins at home - phrasal verb: pass by, look for, look at.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should we use polite words and phrases in a conversation?
sub_strands.core_competences: Communication: The learner’s ability to communicate effectively is developed as they practise clarity in speech through pronunciation of words with the target sounds.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility: Accountability is enhanced as the learner demonstrates dependability when role-playing a telephone conversation, with peers.
sub_strands.pcis: Life Skills: Effective communication is promoted as the learner practises pronouncing words and using polite language in communication.
sub_strands.links: The skill of using polite language in a variety of contexts is relevant in the learning of harmonious living in Religious Education.

outcomes.text: pronounce words with target sounds correctly
use polite words and phrases in a variety of contexts
use a variety of similes, proverbs, idioms and fixed phrases in oral communication
collaborate with peers to judge whether words or phrases have been used politely in a text

skills.name: Use polite expressions: the telephone, interrupting and asking for clarification
skills.mastery: Chooses the polite way to answer a call, to take a message, to interrupt (Excuse me, may I add something?) and to ask for clarification (Could you say that again, please?), and spots a rude or blunt turn, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Interrupts or asks in a blunt way (What? Shut up!).

example.question: Your friend is speaking and you want to add something. What do you say?
example.wrong_answer: Stop! Now it is my turn.
example.correct_answer: Excuse me, may I add something?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Stop! Now it is my turn." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Say excuse me, wait for a pause, and ask.
misconceptions.feedback: A polite interruption begins with Excuse me and asks permission.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Answers the telephone without a greeting or a name.

example.question: You answer your home telephone. What is the best way to begin?
example.correct_answer: Hello, this is Amina speaking. How may I help you?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Who is this?" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Greet, say who you are and offer help.
misconceptions.feedback: On the telephone say hello, say who is speaking and ask how you can help.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Asks for clarification in a rude way (What?).

example.question: You did not hear what the teacher said. What do you say?
example.correct_answer: I beg your pardon. Could you say that again, please?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "What? Say it again." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Ask politely: pardon, could you repeat that, please.
misconceptions.feedback: To ask someone to repeat, say Pardon or Could you say that again, please.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Does not offer to take a message when the person is not in.

example.question: The caller asks for your mother, who is out. What is the polite reply?
example.correct_answer: She is out at the moment. May I take a message?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "She is not here. Bye." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Say where the person is and offer to take a message.
misconceptions.feedback: If the person is out, say so and ask, May I take a message?
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Intensive Reading (Theme 3: Etiquette - telephone)
learning_experiences: skim and scan a text for specific information,
read a text of up to 500 words on etiquette,
answer direct and inferential questions,

skills.name: Use context clues to find the meaning of words, proverbs and similes
skills.mastery: Uses the words around an unfamiliar word, proverb or simile to choose its meaning and says which words gave the clue, in 8 of 10 new passages.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Picks the usual meaning of a word instead of the one that fits.

example.question: In the passage, what does "ran" mean?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "moved fast on foot" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Try each meaning in the sentence.
misconceptions.feedback: Many words have more than one meaning. Try each one in the sentence.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Chooses a meaning because the word looks like another word.

example.question: In the passage, what does the word mean?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a word it looks like" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Use the clues, not how the word looks.
misconceptions.feedback: A word can look like another word and mean something different. Use the clues around it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks the opposite meaning.

example.question: In the passage, what does the word mean?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the opposite" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: See if the sentence says but or because.
misconceptions.feedback: Look at words like but and because. They show whether the word is like or unlike its neighbours.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Picks words that do not explain the word as the clue.

example.question: Which words in the passage help you with the word?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the title" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A clue is close to the word and explains it.
misconceptions.feedback: A clue is a group of words that explains the hard word, usually in the same or the next sentence.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

learning_experiences: identify the pattern: use of show... nominal... how/where/who in a text,
use correlative conjunctions either...or/neither...nor in sentences,
construct sentences using show... nominal... how/where/who,
fill in blanks in provided sentences to practise the use of the pattern how/where/who,
search for instances in which correlative conjunctions either...or/neither are used in newspapers or magazines or the internet.
key_inquiry_questions: Which words do we use when making a choice between two things?

sub_strands.values: Responsibility: This is inculcated as the learner observes safety precautions when searching on the internet for instances in which correlative conjunctions either...or/neither...nor are used.
sub_strands.pcis: Life skills: Effective communication is enhanced as the learner practises the use of correlative conjunctions in a variety of sentences and contexts.

outcomes.text: identify correlative conjunctions in an oral or written text
use correlative conjunctions correctly in oral and written communication
use the pattern show... nominal... how/where/who in sentences
acknowledge the importance of using well-formed sentences in communication

skills.name: Use both ... and, either ... or, neither ... nor and not only ... but also
skills.mastery: Pairs the two halves correctly (both with and, either with or, neither with nor, not only with but also), keeps the verb singular or plural to match, and writes no extra not after neither, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use show or tell me + how, where or who in a sentence
skills.mastery: Writes the question word, then the subject, then the verb (Show me where the library is), without turning the verb round as in a question, in 8 of 10 new sentences.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Writes neither ... or instead of neither ... nor.

example.question: Neither Atieno ___ Juma knew the answer.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "or" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Neither always goes with nor, either with or.
misconceptions.feedback: Neither goes with nor: neither ... nor. Either goes with or.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes both ... or, or both ... nor.

example.question: Both Mary ___ Peter passed the test.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "or" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Both means the two together, so and joins them.
misconceptions.feedback: Both ... and joins two things together. Or is for a choice.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes either ... nor, or either ... and.

example.question: You may either walk ___ take a matatu.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "nor" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Either is a choice, so it goes with or.
misconceptions.feedback: Either gives a choice between two, so it goes with or.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes not only ... and, not only ... also, leaving out but.

example.question: He is not only clever ___ also hardworking.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "and" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The pair is not only ... but also.
misconceptions.feedback: The pair is not only ... but also. Not only ... and is not used.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds not to a neither ... nor sentence (a double negative).

example.question: Neither Ouma nor Wanjiru ___ late.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "was not" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Neither and nor already say no. Do not add not.
misconceptions.feedback: Neither ... nor already means no. Adding not makes a double negative.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Turns the verb round after the question word (Show me where is the library).

example.question: Show me where ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "is the library" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: It is not a question, so the order stays: subject, then verb.
misconceptions.feedback: Inside a sentence the order is not a question order. Say: Show me where the library is.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds do or does after the question word (Tell me how does it work).

example.question: Tell me how ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "does it work" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Leave out do and does here; the verb takes its normal ending.
misconceptions.feedback: After show me or tell me, do not add do or does. Say: Tell me how it works.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the question word (Show me the shop is).

example.question: Please show me ___ the shop is.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "that" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The question word tells what you want to know: where, how or who.
misconceptions.feedback: You need a question word (where, how, who) to say what you want shown.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Ends the sentence with a question mark although it is a request or a statement.

example.question: Tell me who won the race.
example.wrong_answer: Tell me who won the race?
example.correct_answer: Tell me who won the race.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Tell me who won the race?" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A question mark is only for a real question. This sentence tells.
misconceptions.feedback: This sentence asks for something but it is not a question, so it ends with a full stop.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher
