skills.name: Use common abbreviations and acronyms
skills.mastery: Writes and reads the short form of common titles and words (Mr, Dr, etc.), expands Kenyan acronyms (KNEC, KWS, KRA), and tells an abbreviation from an acronym (an acronym is said as a word, like UNICEF), in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: tell an acronym from an abbreviation

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Write numbers in words and figures correctly
skills.mastery: Spells numbers in words (forty, fourteen, ninety, eighth), writes ordinals with the right ending (1st, 2nd, 3rd, 4th), and does not begin a sentence with a figure, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Calls every short form an acronym.

example.question: Which of these is an acronym: Mr, Dr, UNICEF, etc.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Mr" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: An acronym is said as a word. An abbreviation is a short form said letter by letter or in full.
misconceptions.feedback: An acronym is read as a word, like UNICEF. Mr and Dr are abbreviations of longer words.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Expands an acronym with the wrong words.

example.question: What does KNEC stand for?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Kenya National Education Centre" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Each letter is the first letter of a word in the name.
misconceptions.feedback: Each letter stands for a word in the full name. KNEC is the Kenya National Examinations Council.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes etc., e.g. and i.e.

example.question: Which short form means "for example"?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "etc." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Etc. means and so on; e.g. means for example; i.e. means that is.
misconceptions.feedback: E.g. means for example. Etc. means and so on. I.e. means that is.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes the wrong short form of a title or word.

example.question: The short form of Doctor is ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Dc." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Keep the first and last letters or the first letters of the word.
misconceptions.feedback: The short form of Doctor is Dr; of Mister is Mr; of Mistress is Mrs.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes fourty for forty, or forteen and ninty.

example.question: Which is the correct spelling of 40?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "fourty" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Four loses its u in forty, but fourteen keeps it.
misconceptions.feedback: Forty has no u. Fourteen has one: forty, fourteen.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Begins a sentence with a figure.

example.question: Which sentence begins correctly?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "25 learners were absent." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A sentence should not begin with a figure. Spell the number out.
misconceptions.feedback: A sentence does not begin with a figure. Write the number in words: Twenty-five.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes the wrong ending of an ordinal (2th, 3th, 1th).

example.question: The correct way to write second as a figure is ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "2th" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The endings are 1st, 2nd, 3rd, then th for 4th onward.
misconceptions.feedback: Only 1st, 2nd and 3rd have special endings. From 4th the ending is th.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells eighth or ninth wrongly (eigth, nineth).

example.question: Which is the correct spelling of 8th in words?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "eigth" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Eight keeps its t: eighth. Nine loses its e: ninth.
misconceptions.feedback: Eighth has two h-sounds from eight + th. Ninth drops the e of nine.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Pronunciation and Vocabulary (Theme 4: Emergency rescue services)
learning_experiences: pronounce words containing the sound /ʊə/,
say words with same spelling but different meanings,
work with peers to distinguish verbs, nouns and adjectives on the basis of stress, for example, extract/extract, perfect /perfect,
listen to a story related to an emergency and pick out words such as red cross, ambulance, emergency, flying doctors, rescue, security, epidemic, amputate, aid, stroke,
use the identified words in sentences,
work with peers to make a recording of a poetry recitation,
sing a song on emergency rescue services and lay emphasis on content words,
view a video of a recitation of a poem and identify the stressed words,
make recordings as they pronounce words and read sentences while applying the stress correctly,

use expressions such as similes, metaphors, idioms, fixed phrases and proverbs in a written text. apply stress on content words and helping verbs for speech clarity
advocate the correct use of stress in oral communication

skills.name: Use words about emergency and rescue services
skills.mastery: Chooses the right word (ambulance, paramedic, firefighter, siren, evacuate, first aid, emergency, rescue) for a rescue situation, and does not mix the person, the vehicle and the action, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Mixes the vehicle and the person (ambulance and paramedic).

example.question: The ___ gave first aid to the injured man.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "ambulance" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The ambulance is the vehicle; the paramedic is the trained person.
misconceptions.feedback: An ambulance is the vehicle. A paramedic is the trained person who treats the patient.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks evacuate means to rescue a person from fire, not to move people out of a place.

example.question: Everyone had to ___ the building when the alarm rang.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "rescue" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Evacuate: leave a dangerous place. Rescue: save someone in danger.
misconceptions.feedback: Evacuate means to leave a dangerous place. Rescue means to save someone from danger.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong word for a warning sound or sign.

example.question: We heard the ___ of the fire engine from far away.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "alarm" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A siren is the loud warning sound of a vehicle. An alarm warns in a building.
misconceptions.feedback: A siren is the loud sound of an emergency vehicle. An alarm warns people in a building.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use who, whom, whose and which
skills.mastery: Uses who for a person, which for a thing or animal, whose for belonging, and does not add a second pronoun (the boy who he won), in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use someone, anybody, nobody, everything and the like
skills.mastery: Chooses some-, any-, no- or every- with -one, -body or -thing to fit the sentence, uses a singular verb with them, and does not write a double negative (did not see nobody) or noone, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses which for a person (the girl which won).

example.question: The girl ___ won the race is my cousin.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "which" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Who is for people, which is for things and animals.
misconceptions.feedback: Use who for people. Which is for things and animals.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses who for a thing (the book who).

example.question: This is the book ___ I bought yesterday.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "who" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A book is a thing, so which.
misconceptions.feedback: Use which for things. Who is only for people.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses who where whose (belonging) is needed.

example.question: The boy ___ bag was stolen cried.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "who" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The bag belongs to the boy. Belonging is whose.
misconceptions.feedback: When the word shows who something belongs to, use whose.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds a second pronoun (the boy who he won).

example.question: The teacher ___ taught us Maths is kind.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "who she" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The word who already does the work of he or she.
misconceptions.feedback: Who already stands for the person. Do not add he, she or they after it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses who for the object of a verb or after a preposition where whom is needed.

example.question: To ___ did you give the letter?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "who" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After to, with, for, use whom. Whom is for the one who receives.
misconceptions.feedback: After a word like to, with or for, the formal word is whom.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: whom is dropping out of speech

misconceptions.error: Uses any- in a plain statement (I saw anybody).

example.question: I saw ___ at the gate.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "anybody" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: In a plain positive sentence use some-. Any- is for questions and negatives.
misconceptions.feedback: In a plain positive sentence use somebody or someone. Anybody is for questions and negatives.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes a double negative (I did not see nobody).

example.question: I did not meet ___ on the road.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "nobody" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: One negative is enough. After not, use any-.
misconceptions.feedback: Do not use not and nobody together. After not use anybody or anyone.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Uses a plural verb after everyone or everybody.

example.question: Everyone ___ here.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "are" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Everyone sounds like many, but the word is singular.
misconceptions.feedback: Everyone, everybody and nobody are singular, so they take is and has.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes noone or no-one as one word.

example.question: There was ___ in the hall.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "noone" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: No one is two words. Nobody is one word.
misconceptions.feedback: Write no one as two words, or use the one word nobody.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Functional Writing (Theme 4: Emergency rescue services)
learning_experiences: go through a sample formal letter and identify its components,
search and download samples of formal letters online,
collaborate to plan a formal invitation letter,
write the formal letter individually,
proofread the letter and make corrections,
display the letter in the classroom, noticeboard or posters,
upload the invitation letter online or send through email, WhatsApp, among others, to peers,

write an invitation letter to the County NTSA Officer, Red Cross or St. John Ambulance representative and requesting for a talk on emergency response to your schools, scouts movement, Red Cross or St. John Ambulance club.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do you write letters?
Which kinds of letters do you write?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Collaboration: The learner’s ability to work with others is enhanced as they collaborate to plan a formal invitation letter.
Digital Literacy: The learner’s ability to interact with technological devices is enhanced as they access learning materials in digital platforms by searching for sample letters online and downloading them.
sub_strands.values: Responsibility: This is enhanced as the learner engages in assigned roles when proofreading the letter and making corrections.
sub_strands.pcis: Health and Safety (Online Safety): The learner observes online safety as they upload the invitation letter online or send through email, WhatsApp, among others, to peers.
sub_strands.links: The skill of writing invitation letters is related to the writing of letters in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify the key features of a formal letter
create a formal invitation letter using the correct format
judge a formal letter for correctness of language and relevance

skills.name: Know the features of a formal letter and invitation
skills.mastery: Tells where each part goes (address, date, greeting, subject line, closing, signature), matches the closing to the greeting (Dear Sir with Yours faithfully), and picks the polite formal wording, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: choose the part or its place

misconceptions.error: Closes Dear Sir with Yours sincerely, or Dear Mr Otieno with Yours faithfully.

example.question: A letter begins "Dear Sir". How should it end?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Yours sincerely" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Dear Sir or Madam goes with faithfully. A named person goes with sincerely.
misconceptions.feedback: Dear Sir or Madam ends with Yours faithfully. Dear Mr Otieno (a name) ends with Yours sincerely.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses friendly language in a formal letter.

example.question: Which line is right for a formal invitation?
example.wrong_answer: Hi! Come to our party, it will be fun.
example.correct_answer: You are kindly invited to our school open day.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Hi! Come to our party, it will be fun." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A formal letter is polite and plain, with no slang or short forms.
misconceptions.feedback: A formal letter uses polite, full sentences. No slang and no short forms like it'll.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the writer's address in the wrong place.

example.question: Where does the writer's address go in a formal letter?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "at the bottom" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The sender's address begins the letter, at the top right.
misconceptions.feedback: The writer's address goes at the top right. The receiver's address goes under it on the left.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the subject line.

example.question: Which part tells the reader what the letter is about?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the closing" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The subject heading comes under the greeting.
misconceptions.feedback: The subject line sits below the greeting and tells the reader the topic in a few words.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes the name but no signature or forgets the position.

example.question: Where does the signature go?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "above the greeting" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Greeting, body, closing, then signature and name.
misconceptions.feedback: The signature goes under the closing, with the full name printed under it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Pronunciation and Vocabulary (Theme 5: Our tourist attractions)
learning_experiences: listen to correct pronunciation of sounds, words, and phrases from the teacher, audio-visual recordings among others,
work with peers to say words and phrases with the sounds /ð / and /θ / and assist one another,
listen to a poem on tourist attraction sites in Kenya and recite it.
respond to questions on the poem,

use the following expressions in sentences: fixed phrases: make friends, be careful, fall asleep, in future, in a hurry simile: as brave as a lion; as blind as a bat metaphor: She is a lion. She is so brave proverbs: Prevention is better than cure, seeing is believing, the early bird catches the worm idioms: Sick as a dog, you are what you eat, kick the habit, let the cat out of the bag, would not hurt a fly phrasal verbs: Go away, go back, pick up, get away...the antelope got away from the lion.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should we pronounce sounds correctly?
What information do we obtain when we listen keenly?

Citizenship: The learner’s sense of patriotism is enhanced as they develop interest in socio-cultural and economic activities by interacting with poems on Kenya’s tourist attraction sites.
Self-efficacy: The learner’s ability to pay attention to detail is brought out as they use varied expressions in sentences to express themselves.
sub_strands.values: Social Justice: This is inculcated as the learner assists others to say words and phrases with the sounds /ð / and /θ/ without discrimination.
sub_strands.pcis: Wildlife and tourism: This is promoted as the learners are exposed to information on our tourist attraction sites by listening to poems on the theme.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the vocabulary learnt to similar content in Social Studies.

outcomes.text: listen for specific information and the main idea for self-expression
respond to oral questions based on the theme
use expressions such as similes, metaphors and proverbs in oral communication
advocate the importance of listening comprehension

learning_experiences: preview a text by focusing on the title, author, among others (fiction/ non-fiction) 1251- 1500 words),
collaborate to determine the appropriateness of a reading text,
skim texts on the theme of tourist attraction sites in Kenya to find out the general idea,
scan a text to find specific details such as key words,
select and read an appropriate reading material based on their interest.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should we read a variety of materials?
How do you identify the book you want to read?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Learning to Learn: The learner’s ability to grasp information is enhanced as they interact with a variety of texts.
Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: The learner’s ability to solve simple problems is developed through selection and reading of appropriate texts based on their interest.

sub_strands.pcis: Patriotism: This is advocated for as the learner is exposed to information on our tourist attraction sites by reading texts on the said theme.
sub_strands.links: The skill of extensive reading is appropriate in the learning and study of Agriculture.

outcomes.text: select appropriate reading materials from varied texts
read a variety of texts for enjoyment and general understanding
assess a text for appropriateness and relevance

sub_strands.sub_strand: Adjectives (Theme 5: Our tourist attractions)
learning_experiences: identify adjectives in print and digital texts,
compare items using simple, comparative and superlative forms of adjectives,
collaborate with peers to make a list of regular and irregular adjectives,
create a crossword puzzle and a word search, using comparative and superlative adjectives,
display the completed crossword puzzle and word search on posters or charts.
key_inquiry_questions: Which words do we use to describe people, things, and places?
How do we compare people, things, and events?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Self-efficacy: The learner’s ability to plan efficiently is developed as they create and display the crossword puzzles and word search.
Digital Literacy: The learner’s ability to manipulate digital devices is improved as they share work accomplished (crossword puzzles and word search) on posters and charts.

outcomes.text: identify simple, comparative and superlative forms of adjectives in print and digital texts correctly
use simple, comparative and superlative forms of adjectives in oral and written texts
acknowledge the importance of using adjectives correctly in communication

skills.name: Use the simple, comparative and superlative forms of adjectives
skills.mastery: Tells the three forms apart and writes as ... as with the simple form, than with the comparative and the with the superlative, and does not write as taller as or the tallest than, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses the comparative inside as ... as (as taller as).

example.question: Kamau is as ___ as his brother.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "taller" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Between as ... as use the plain adjective.
misconceptions.feedback: In as ... as, use the plain form: as tall as, not as taller as.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses than with a superlative (the tallest than).

example.question: Wanjiru is the tallest girl ___ the class.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "than" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Than goes with a comparative (taller than). With the tallest use in or of.
misconceptions.feedback: Than goes with the comparative. After the tallest use in or of: the tallest in the class.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the before a superlative.

example.question: Otieno is ___ fastest runner in Grade 6.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "(nothing)" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A superlative picks one from a group and needs the.
misconceptions.feedback: A superlative needs the before it: the fastest, the most careful.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out than after a comparative (Juma is taller Peter).

example.question: Juma is taller ___ Peter.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "from" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After a comparative the word is than.
misconceptions.feedback: After a comparative adjective use than, not from or that.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes one of the tallest girl instead of girls.

example.question: She is one of the tallest ___ in the school.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "girl" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: One of the ... needs a plural noun: there are many tallest girls and she is one.
misconceptions.feedback: After one of the + superlative, use a plural noun: one of the tallest girls.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Creative Writing (Theme 5: Our tourist attractions)
learning_experiences: identify the parts of a narrative composition,
work with peers to plan a narrative composition of about 160-200 words,
read sample narrative compositions with peers and critique them for: - correctness of language - flow or organisation of ideas - relevance to the topic - creativity
use the steps of the writing process to create a narrative composition of about (160 - 200 words), on tourist attraction sites,

use appropriate fixed phrases such as: catch fire; similes such as: as fast as lightning; metaphors such as: the boy was a fox. He was so cunning; proverbs such as: prevention is better than cure; idioms such as get into hot water; and phrasal verbs such as care for.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should we organise ideas in our compositions?
How can you make your writing interesting?

Communication: The learner’s ability to communicate effectively is developed as they practise the skills of writing clearly by following the stages of the writing process and creating a narrative composition.
Creativity and Imagination: The learner’s artistic skills are enhanced as they create and write narrative compositions.
sub_strands.values: Unity: Cooperation is displayed as the learner collaborates with peers to plan a narrative composition.

outcomes.text: plan a narrative composition collaboratively
organise ideas coherently, clearly, and logically for writing fluency
create a narrative composition on a variety of topics
judge a narrative composition for correctness of language, relevance of the topic and organisation of ideas

sub_strands.sub_strand: Pronunciation and Vocabulary (Theme 6: Jobs and occupation - work ethics)
learning_experiences: say sounds, words, phrases, and sentences with the sounds /f/, /v/ and /əʊ/,
say tongue twisters with the sounds /f/ and /v/ and /əʊ/,
watch a video of a dialogue on work ethics and imitate the use of stress and intonation by the speakers,
recite a choral verse, with peers,
sing songs featuring stress and intonation,

form sentences using the following expressions: fixed phrases: Take care of, have no idea, you never know simile: As happy as king, as busy as a bee, work like a horse metaphor: Wambui is a bee. She is so busy. idioms: Lay off, hand in, take over, deal with, strike while the iron is hot, go the extra mile proverbs: Make hay while the sun shines. The sun does not wait for a king, Honesty is the best policy, Slow but sure wins the race, Jack of all trades, master of none phrasal verbs: grow up, take over, deal with, give up, go on.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do we put emphasis on some words and not others?
How can you vary your voice to convey different meanings?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication: The learner’s ability to speak clearly and effectively is enhanced through practice and saying tongue twisters with the sounds /f/, /v/ and /əʊ/.
Self-efficacy: The learner’s ability to analyse is developed when they give their views as they form sentences using the given expressions.
sub_strands.values: Integrity: This is enhanced as the learner practises accountability through watching a video of a dialogue on work ethics and imitating the use of stress and intonation by the speakers.
sub_strands.pcis: Career Guidance: The learner’s grasp of careers is enhanced as they interact with information on work ethics by watching a dialogue.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the concept of stress and intonation to their learning in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify words and phrases with the sounds /f/, /v/ and /əʊ/
use vocabulary related to the theme in sentences correctly
apply stress and intonation in questions, statements, and exclamatory sentences
value the importance of stress and intonation in sentences

skills.name: Choose words by their sound: /ɪə/, /ʊə/, /əʊ/, /f/, /v/ and /h/
skills.mastery: Picks the word with the same vowel sound as near (/ɪə/), tour (/ʊə/) or go (/əʊ/), or the word that starts with /f/, /v/ or an /h/ that is said (hour and honest start without it), in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: pick the word with the same sound

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Chooses by spelling and not by sound (bear for near).

example.question: Which word has the same vowel sound as "near"?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "bear" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Say both words aloud. Do they sound alike?
misconceptions.feedback: Spelling can mislead. Say the words aloud: near and beer share the vowel sound, bear does not.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: sound judgements depend on the accent the class is taught in

misconceptions.error: Mixes /f/ and /v/ (fan and van).

example.question: Which word starts with the sound /v/?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "fan" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: For /v/ the upper teeth touch the lower lip and the voice hums; for /f/ it does not.
misconceptions.feedback: For /v/ the voice hums with your teeth on your lip. For /f/ there is only air.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: sound judgements depend on the accent the class is taught in

misconceptions.error: Says the h in hour and honest, or drops it in house.

example.question: Which word does NOT start with the sound /h/?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "house" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: In hour, honest and heir the h is silent.
misconceptions.feedback: In hour, honest and heir the h is silent, so they start with a vowel sound. In house and hand it is said.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: sound judgements depend on the accent the class is taught in

misconceptions.error: Treats /ʊə/ and /ɔː/ as one sound (tour, more).

example.question: Which word has the same vowel sound as "tour"?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "more" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Tour, poor and pure share one sound. More, door and floor share another.
misconceptions.feedback: Tour, poor and pure share the sound /ʊə/. More, door and floor share a different sound.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: sound judgements depend on the accent the class is taught in

sub_strands.sub_strand: Intensive Reading (Theme 6: Jobs and occupation - work ethics)
learning_experiences: relate the title and illustrations/pictures with their personal experiences.
skim a text to obtain a general idea (dialogue of about 500 words),
scan a text on work ethics for specific details,
observe the cover, pictures, and read the title to make predictions,

create mental images (visualise) from read, viewed, or heard text,
retell events in a story/dialogue in their own words,
work with peers to make posters featuring the new words he or she has learnt,
answer literal and inferential questions.

How can you predict what will happen in a story or passage?

use contextual clues to infer the meaning of vocabulary such as words, proverbs, fixed phrases, similes, and phrasal verbs
respond to a reading text for comprehension
acknowledge the role of reading comprehension in lifelong learning

learning_experiences: work with peers to view a video or listen to an audio text on work ethics featuring phrasal quantifiers and identify them,
make sentences using phrasal quantifiers such as a lot of..., a pinch of... plenty of..., a number of, a crate of ...,
create charts and posters using phrasal quantifiers and share them on the school notice board or social media,

Which words are used to show the amount of something?

Communication: The learner’s ability for self-expression is developed through creating posters using phrasal quantifiers.

sub_strands.pcis: Career exploration: The learner’s knowledge on careers is enhanced as they interact with information on the theme when working with peers to view a video or listen to an audio text on work ethics featuring phrasal quantifiers.

use phrasal quantifiers with countable and uncountable nouns correctly
judge the correctness of phrasal quantifiers in sentences

skills.name: Use a number of, a great deal of, plenty of and a piece of with the right noun
skills.mastery: Uses a number of and a good many with countable nouns, a great deal of and an amount of with uncountable nouns, and a piece, bottle, loaf or bar of for single items of an uncountable thing, with of every time, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses a number of with an uncountable noun (a number of water).

example.question: A number of ___ were late.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "water" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A number of needs things we can count.
misconceptions.feedback: A number of goes with countable nouns, such as learners or books, not with water or sugar.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses a great deal of or an amount of with countable nouns.

example.question: We used a great deal of ___ for the cake.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "eggs" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A great deal of is for things we cannot count one by one.
misconceptions.feedback: A great deal of and an amount of go with uncountable nouns such as flour, water and advice.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds -s to the uncountable noun (a piece of advices).

example.question: He gave me a piece of ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "advices" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Advice, news and furniture never take -s. Count them with a piece of.
misconceptions.feedback: Advice, news, information and furniture have no plural. Say a piece of advice.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out of (a loaf bread).

example.question: Mama bought a loaf ___ bread.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "(nothing)" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The pattern is a loaf OF bread, a bar OF soap.

skills.name: Use the future continuous: will be + verb-ing

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Leaves out be (will travelling).

example.question: This time tomorrow we ___ travelling to Kisumu.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "will" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The future continuous is will + be + verb-ing.
misconceptions.feedback: The future continuous needs be: will be travelling. Will travelling is not complete.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes will been or will being.

example.question: At six o'clock I ___ cooking supper.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "will been" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After will, the verb be stays in its plain form: will be.
misconceptions.feedback: After will use the plain form be, not been or being: will be cooking.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the present continuous for a future time (is travelling tomorrow at noon).

example.question: At noon tomorrow Mama ___ working in the shamba.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "is" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A future time word asks for will be.
misconceptions.feedback: When the time is in the future, use will be + verb-ing, not is or are.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes will be with the plain verb (will be travel).

example.question: Tomorrow at ten the pupils ___ writing a test.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "will write" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The pattern is will be + verb-ing, a continuing action.
misconceptions.feedback: The future continuous ends in -ing: will be writing. Will be write is not correct.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

collaborate with peers to determine the correct use of the comma and the double quotation marks

skills.name: Use the comma
skills.mastery: Puts the comma between items in a list, after an opening word or phrase, round extra information and before or after spoken words, and does not put one between subject and verb or use it to join two sentences, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use double quotation marks for direct speech
skills.mastery: Puts double quotation marks round the exact words spoken, closes them after the punctuation, keeps the capital letter at the start of the speech and the small letter after said in split speech, and does not use them for reported speech, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Puts a comma between a subject and its verb.

example.question: Which sentence is correct?
example.wrong_answer: The boy in the blue shirt, is my cousin.
example.correct_answer: The boy in the blue shirt is my cousin.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "The boy in the blue shirt, is my cousin." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Read it: a comma does not come between who and what they do.
misconceptions.feedback: Do not put a comma between a subject and its verb.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the commas in a list.

example.question: Which sentence is correct?
example.wrong_answer: Mama bought rice beans maize and sugar.
example.correct_answer: Mama bought rice, beans, maize and sugar.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Mama bought rice beans maize and sugar." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Put a comma after every item except the last two joined by and.
misconceptions.feedback: In a list, put a comma between the items. And stands before the last one.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the comma after an opening word or phrase.

example.question: Which sentence is correct?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "After lunch we played football." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A phrase at the start of the sentence is followed by a comma.
misconceptions.feedback: When a sentence opens with a word or phrase such as After lunch, put a comma after it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Joins two full sentences with only a comma.

example.question: Which sentence is correct?
example.wrong_answer: It was raining, we stayed at home.
example.correct_answer: It was raining, so we stayed at home.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It was raining, we stayed at home." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Two sentences need a full stop or a joining word as well as the comma.
misconceptions.feedback: A comma alone cannot join two sentences. Add a joining word such as so, or use a full stop.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the comma that separates the speaker from the words.

example.question: Which sentence is correct?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Mama said "Come and eat."" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A comma goes between said and the opening quotation mark.
misconceptions.feedback: Put a comma between the speaker and the spoken words: Mama said, "Come and eat."
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes direct speech with no quotation marks.

example.question: Which sentence is correct?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Mama said, Come and eat." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The exact words spoken go inside double quotation marks.
misconceptions.feedback: Put double quotation marks round the exact words someone says.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts the full stop or question mark outside the closing marks.

example.question: Which sentence is correct?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Juma asked, "Where is my bag?"." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The mark that ends the speech goes inside the quotation marks.
misconceptions.feedback: The question mark, full stop or exclamation mark goes inside the closing quotation marks.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Starts the second part of split speech with a capital letter.

example.question: Which sentence is correct?
example.wrong_answer: "I am tired," said Amina, "But I will finish."
example.correct_answer: "I am tired," said Amina, "but I will finish."

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer ""I am tired," said Amina, "But I will finish."" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: It is one sentence cut in two. The second part has a small letter.
misconceptions.feedback: In split speech the second part is a small letter because the sentence goes on.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts quotation marks round reported speech.

example.question: Which sentence is correct?
example.correct_answer: She said that she was tired.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "She said that "she was tired."" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Quotation marks are for the exact words only. Reported speech is not exact.
misconceptions.feedback: Reported speech does not use quotation marks. Use them only for the exact words spoken.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses single quotation marks where the design asks for double.

example.question: Which sentence is correct?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Mama said, 'Come and eat.'" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: In your school use double quotation marks for speech.
misconceptions.feedback: In Kenyan school English the usual marks for speech are double quotation marks.
misconceptions.source: to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher: single marks are also correct British style

skills.mastery: Says that a riddle asks a puzzle with a hidden answer and a proverb gives advice or a truth, and answers a simple riddle by what it describes, not by the words in it, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Use phrasal verbs: put up with, cope with, agree with, give up
skills.mastery: Chooses the phrasal verb and its particle for a meaning (give up, set off, break down, run out of, put up with, cope with, agree with, look after), and does not use the wrong preposition, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Calls a proverb a riddle.

example.question: Which of these is a riddle?
example.wrong_answer: Slow and steady wins the race.
example.correct_answer: What has a neck but no head?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Slow and steady wins the race." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A riddle asks a question and waits for an answer.
misconceptions.feedback: A riddle is a puzzle with an answer to find. A proverb gives advice and has no answer to find.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Calls a riddle a proverb.

example.question: Which of these is a proverb?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "What runs but never walks?" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A proverb tells us what to do or what is true.
misconceptions.feedback: A proverb teaches a lesson. A riddle asks something that you must guess.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Answers a riddle from the words and not the description.

example.question: I have a neck but no head. What am I?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a giraffe" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Think: what has a neck but no head and a mouth?
misconceptions.feedback: A riddle describes an object in a puzzling way. Match all the clues, not the first word.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks a riddle is just a story with no answer.

example.question: What is special about a riddle?
example.correct_answer: It has a hidden answer to guess.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "It tells a long story." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Riddles end with a puzzle: the listener answers.
misconceptions.feedback: A riddle always has an answer to find. It is not a story.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Reads a phrasal verb word for word.

example.question: What does "put up with" mean?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "put something on top" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The particle changes the verb's meaning.
misconceptions.feedback: A phrasal verb has its own meaning. Put up with means to bear something patiently.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong particle (give in for give up).

example.question: He did not ___ trying until he passed.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "give in" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Give up: stop trying. Give in: say yes after refusing.
misconceptions.feedback: Each particle makes a new meaning. Give up means stop trying; give in means agree after refusing.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong preposition after the phrasal verb (agree to, cope in).

example.question: I agree ___ you.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "to" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Agree with a person. Cope with a problem.
misconceptions.feedback: Say agree WITH a person and cope WITH a problem.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks break down and break up mean the same.

example.question: The old matatu ___ on the way to Nairobi.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "broke up" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Broke down: stopped working. Broke up: split apart or ended.
misconceptions.feedback: Break down means stop working. Break up means to come apart or to end.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use say and tell, borrow and lend, bring and take, learn and teach, hear and listen, see and look correctly
skills.mastery: Chooses between each of these pairs from who is giving, who is receiving and which way the thing moves, and does not use one word for both as in Kiswahili, in 8 of 10 new items.

misconceptions.error: Leaves out be in a passive sentence (The window broken by the wind).

example.question: The window ___ by the wind.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "broken" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A passive needs be + the past participle.
misconceptions.feedback: A passive sentence needs a form of be before the past participle: was broken, is written.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the simple past instead of the past participle (was wrote, was ate).

example.question: The letter was ___ by Mary.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "wrote" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After was or were use the participle: written, eaten, broken, taken.
misconceptions.feedback: After was or were use the past participle: was written, was eaten, was taken.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Does not match was or were to the subject (The books was returned).

example.question: The books ___ returned on Friday.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "was" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The subject is plural, so use were.
misconceptions.feedback: The be-word must match the subject: the book was returned, the books were returned.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Calls an active sentence passive because it is in the past.

example.question: Which sentence is passive?
example.correct_answer: The rice was cooked by Wanjiku.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Wanjiku cooked the rice." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Ask: does the subject do the action or receive it?
misconceptions.feedback: In a passive sentence the subject RECEIVES the action. In Wanjiku cooked the rice, Wanjiku does it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Turns the sentence round but keeps the doer as the subject.

example.question: Passive of: Baraka kicked the ball.
example.wrong_answer: Baraka was kicked by the ball.
example.correct_answer: The ball was kicked by Baraka.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Baraka was kicked by the ball." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The thing acted on moves to the front.
misconceptions.feedback: In the passive, the thing that receives the action goes first: The ball was kicked by Baraka.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses say and tell for each other (She said me; He told that).

example.question: The teacher ___ us a story.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "said" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Tell takes a person straight after it (tell us). Say does not.
misconceptions.feedback: Tell is followed by the person (told us). Say is followed by the words (said that).
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Uses borrow and lend for each other.

example.question: Please ___ me your pen.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "borrow" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Lend: you give it for a short time. Borrow: you take it for a short time.
misconceptions.feedback: You borrow FROM someone and you lend TO someone. Please lend me your pen.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Uses bring and take for each other.

example.question: Please ___ this letter to the headteacher's office.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "bring" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Bring: towards the speaker. Take: away from the speaker.
misconceptions.feedback: Bring means to carry it toward the speaker. Take means to carry it away from the speaker.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Uses learn and teach for each other.

example.question: Mr Kimani will ___ us fractions.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "learn" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The teacher teaches. The pupil learns.
misconceptions.feedback: The teacher TEACHES and the pupil LEARNS.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Uses hear and listen for each other.

example.question: Please ___ carefully to the story.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "hear" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Listen: you try to hear. Hear: it reaches your ears.
misconceptions.feedback: You hear without trying, but you LISTEN on purpose. Listen is followed by to.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses see, look and watch for each other.

example.question: ___ at the bird on the roof.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "See" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Look is on purpose, and it takes at. See is what your eyes find.
misconceptions.feedback: Look is on purpose and takes at (look at). See is what your eyes find. Watch is to look at something that moves.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Creative Writing (Theme 8: The farm – animal safety and care)
learning_experiences: collaborate to use the writing process (planning, drafting, editing, revising, and publishing) and create a narrative composition of about (160-200 words),
identify idioms, proverbs, and similes from an oral or written text,
use appropriate words and expressions such as fixed phrases: similes, idioms phrasal verbs and metaphors in their writing,
display their compositions in class, on charts, school magazine, noticeboard and blogs, among others,
complete a gap-filling exercise involving similes, proverbs, and idioms.

What makes a composition interesting?

Creativity and Imagination: The learner’s ability to come up with new ideas is enhanced while creating narrative compositions.

use proverbs, phrasal verbs and idiomatic expressions in writing
create a narrative composition based on a given theme for self-expression
judge a narrative composition for creativity, organisation of ideas, relevance of topic, and correctness

recite poems on lifestyle diseases with words which have the sounds /eə/ /aʊ/ and /h/,
speak at the right speed,

sub_strands.values:
Responsibility: This is cultivated in the learner as they undertake assigned roles while delivering speeches on lifestyle diseases.

sub_strands.pcis: Lifestyle diseases: The learner’s grasp of health issues is enhanced as they make short speeches on lifestyle diseases expressively, accurately and without hesitations.

outcomes.text: identify words, phrases and sentences with the target sounds
use words and expressions such as idioms, proverbs and similes related to the theme in sentences correctly
make an oral presentation related to the theme fluently

picture events, characters or places in their minds,
read texts of up to 500 words related to the selected theme,
connect events in a text with an occurrence in their own life or real world events,
use the image on the front cover to predict events in the text,

retell the events depicted in a text in their own words.
answer direct and inferential questions from a variety of texts,

create mental images from viewed, heard or read text for comprehension
respond to texts correctly for comprehension
acknowledge the importance of reading comprehension in lifelong learning

skills.name: Tell a fact from an opinion, and a story from information
skills.mastery: Says that a fact can be checked and an opinion says what someone thinks or feels (best, beautiful, should), and tells whether a short text is a made-up story or information, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Takes an opinion as a fact.

example.question: Which is a fact?
example.correct_answer: Githeri is made from maize and beans.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Githeri is the best food." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A fact can be checked. Words like best, nicest and should show an opinion.
misconceptions.feedback: An opinion says what someone thinks. Words like best and nicest show an opinion. A fact can be checked.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Takes a fact as an opinion.

example.question: Which is an opinion?
example.wrong_answer: Nairobi is the capital of Kenya.
example.correct_answer: Nairobi is the most exciting city.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Nairobi is the capital of Kenya." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Can you check it? Then it is a fact.
misconceptions.feedback: A fact can be checked. Nairobi is the capital is a fact; the most exciting is a feeling.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Calls a made-up story information.

example.question: Is this text a story or information?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "information" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A story has made-up characters and events.
misconceptions.feedback: A story is made up, with characters and events. Information gives facts.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Use adverbs of manner, time, place, frequency and degree
skills.mastery: Tells what an adverb shows, uses well (not good), hard and hardly with their right meanings, puts the adverb of frequency before the main verb (always goes), and does not use an adjective after a verb of action, in 8 of 10 new items.
question_forms: say what the adverb tells us

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses an adjective after an action verb (He runs quick).

example.question: The boy runs ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "quick" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: How does he run? An -ly word tells how.
misconceptions.feedback: A word that tells HOW something is done is an adverb, usually ending in -ly: quickly, slowly.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Writes good where well is needed (She sings good).

example.question: Wanjiru sings very ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "good" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Good describes a noun (a good song). Well describes a verb (sings well).
misconceptions.feedback: Good is an adjective. Well is the adverb of good: a good singer, sings well.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Thinks hardly means with great effort.

example.question: He worked ___ and passed the exam.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "hardly" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Hard means with effort. Hardly means almost not at all.
misconceptions.feedback: Hard means with much effort. Hardly means almost not: He hardly slept means he slept very little.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Puts a frequency adverb in the wrong place (He goes always).

example.question: Juma ___ walks to school.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "walks always" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Always, never, often and usually go before the main verb.
misconceptions.feedback: Frequency adverbs such as always, never and often come before the main verb: he always walks.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Names the wrong kind of adverb (calls yesterday an adverb of place).

example.question: What does the adverb "yesterday" tell us?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "place" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Ask: how, when, where or how often?
misconceptions.feedback: Yesterday tells WHEN, so it is an adverb of time. Where tells place; how tells manner; how often tells frequency.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Mechanics of writing (Theme 9: Lifestyle diseases)
learning_experiences: search for and share with peers hyphenated and unhyphenated words such as dark-blue shirt, good-looking, goodhearted, fast-moving, anticlockwise from the internet, magazines, newspapers, textbooks or brochures,
listen to a dictation of the following words: mother-in-law, father-in-law, sister-in-law, brother-in law and write them down,
listen to an audio recording of the words mother-in-law, father-in-law, sister-in-law, brother-in-law and anti-clockwise and create a list,
use words such as fast-flowing, slow-moving, open-mouthed, big-eyed, sugar-free among others in sentences,
hyphenate words which refer to age such as five- year-old girl, two-year-old and middle-aged man,
use the hyphen correctly when writing numbers 21 through 99: for example, twenty-one; ninety-nine
work with peers to create a poster on lifestyle diseases featuring the words learnt, Note: The learner should only be exposed to simple and common hyphenated words.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is it important to punctuate texts appropriately?

Unity: This is displayed in the team spirit that is inculcated in the learner as they work with peers to create a poster on lifestyle diseases.
sub_strands.pcis: Lifestyle Diseases: The learner’s general health and wellbeing is improved as they interact with, and gain knowledge on lifestyle diseases while creating posters featuring the target words.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the learning of punctuation marks (the hyphen) to correct punctuation of texts in Agriculture.

outcomes.text: identify grade appropriate hyphenated words from a written text
use grade appropriate hyphenated words correctly for clarity of meaning
judge sentences for correctness of language, and use of the hyphen

skills.name: Use the hyphen in compound words and numbers
skills.mastery: Writes the hyphen in compound words (well-known, mother-in-law), in numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine and in a compound before a noun (a ten-year-old boy, but ten years old), and does not write ten-years-old, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Leaves out the hyphen in a compound before a noun (a well known singer).

example.question: Which sentence is correct?
example.wrong_answer: She is a well known singer.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "She is a well known singer." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Two words that work as one describing word before a noun take a hyphen.
misconceptions.feedback: A compound that describes the noun after it takes a hyphen: a well-known singer.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes twenty one or twentyone.

example.question: Which is correct?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "twenty one" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The numbers 21 to 99 in words take a hyphen.
misconceptions.feedback: Numbers from twenty-one to ninety-nine are hyphenated when written in words.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Makes the number plural inside a compound (a ten-years-old boy).

example.question: Which sentence is correct?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "He is a ten-years-old boy." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: In a compound before a noun, the unit stays singular.
misconceptions.feedback: Before a noun, the unit is singular: a ten-year-old boy. Without the hyphen: he is ten years old.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes mother in law or motherinlaw for mother-in-law.

example.question: Which is correct?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "mother in law" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Words for relations by marriage are hyphenated.
misconceptions.feedback: Words such as mother-in-law and sister-in-law are written with hyphens.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Join ideas with although, unless, while, so that, until and whereas
skills.mastery: Chooses the conjunction that fits the meaning (contrast, condition, purpose, time), uses only one joining word (Although ... but ... is wrong), and does not write unless ... not, in 8 of 10 new items.

misconceptions.error: Uses although and but in the same sentence.

example.question: ___ it rained, we played outside.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Although" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Use one joining word only: although OR but.
misconceptions.feedback: Do not use although and but together. Although it rained, we played. Or: It rained but we played.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Writes unless not.

example.question: You will not pass ___ you study.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "unless not" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Unless already means if not.
misconceptions.feedback: Unless means if not, so do not add not: You will fail unless you study.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses while or until where the meaning needs the other.

example.question: Wait here ___ I come back.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "while" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Until: up to the time that. While: at the same time as.
misconceptions.feedback: Until means up to the time that something happens. While means at the same time as.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses so that for a reason that already happened.

example.question: We left early ___ we could catch the bus.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "because" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: So that tells the purpose: what you want to happen next.
misconceptions.feedback: So that gives the purpose: the aim you want. Because gives the reason for something that has happened.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses because or so where a contrast is meant (whereas).

example.question: Kamau likes tea, ___ his sister prefers milk.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "because" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Two different things side by side: whereas.
misconceptions.feedback: Whereas and while show two things that are different. Because shows a reason.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Ask questions with whose, which, whom, how often, how long and how far
skills.mastery: Chooses the question word that fits the answer given (whose for owner, which for a choice from a set, how often for frequency, how long for time, how far for distance), in 8 of 10 new questions.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses who where whose (belonging) is asked.

example.question: ___ bag is this?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Who" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The answer is an owner: Wanjiru's. That is whose.
misconceptions.feedback: Ask whose when you want to know who owns something.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses what where which is needed for a choice from a small set.

example.question: ___ of these two books is yours?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "What" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Which is for a choice from a small number you can see.
misconceptions.feedback: Use which when the choice is from a small set; use what when anything is possible.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses how much for things you can count, or how many for things you cannot.

example.question: How ___ eggs did you buy?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "much" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Count them? how many. Cannot count them? how much.
misconceptions.feedback: How many is for things you can count (eggs). How much is for things you cannot (milk, money).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes how long (time) with how far (distance).

example.question: ___ is it from Nakuru to Naivasha?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "How long" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Distance is how far. How long can be time.
misconceptions.feedback: How far asks about distance. How long asks about time or length.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses when where how often is asked.

example.question: ___ do you go to the library? Twice a week.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "When" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Twice a week tells how many times. That is how often.
misconceptions.feedback: How often asks how many times. When asks at what time.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher
