skills.name: Choose synonyms and antonyms
skills.mastery: Chooses a word with the same meaning (synonym) or the opposite meaning (antonym) in a sentence, and does not give a related word, the same word or the wrong kind of pair, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Gives a word with the same meaning when the opposite is asked.

example.question: The old man was weak but his son was ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "feeble" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Antonym means opposite. Ask: is it the same meaning or the opposite?
misconceptions.feedback: An antonym is a word with the OPPOSITE meaning. Feeble means weak, not the opposite of weak.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives an opposite when a word with the same meaning is asked.

example.question: Wafula was delighted with his gift. He was very ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "sad" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Synonym means same meaning. Delighted means very pleased.
misconceptions.feedback: A synonym has the SAME meaning. Delighted means very pleased, so happy is the synonym.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives a related word that is neither the same nor the opposite.

example.question: The road was wide but the path was ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "long" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Think of the exact opposite of wide, not any word about roads.
misconceptions.feedback: Choose the word that is the exact opposite. Long is about something else; the opposite of wide is narrow.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Repeats the same word as the answer.

example.question: The soup was hot, but the juice was ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "hot" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The answer must be a different word.
misconceptions.feedback: An antonym is a different word with the opposite meaning, not the same word again.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Find rhyme, repeated lines and rhythm in a poem or song
skills.mastery: Finds the words that rhyme by sound (not by spelling), the line that repeats and the words a poem stresses, in 8 of 10 new poems.

prerequisites.reason: This skill builds on it. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Chooses words that end with the same letters but do not sound alike (cough, rough).

example.question: Which two words rhyme?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "cough and rough" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Rhyme is sound, not spelling. Say the words aloud.
misconceptions.feedback: Rhyming words sound alike at the end. Cough and rough end with the same letters but do not rhyme.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Takes repetition for rhyme.

example.question: Which line repeats in the poem?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the first line" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Repeated lines are the same words again, not just similar sounds.
misconceptions.feedback: A repeated line is the same line again. Rhyme is a similar sound at the ends.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Looks only at the first word of each line.

example.question: Which words rhyme?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the first words of lines" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Rhymes are usually at the end of lines.
misconceptions.feedback: Rhyming words are usually the last words of the lines.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

skills.name: Form question tags with be, have, do and modal verbs
skills.mastery: Adds the right tag to a statement: the same helper verb with the opposite sign and a pronoun (is/isn't, has/hasn't, does/doesn't, can/can't, will/won't), and writes aren't I after I am, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses a tag with the same sign as the statement (She is tall, is she?).

example.question: Wafula is a good singer, ___?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "is he" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A positive statement takes a negative tag.
misconceptions.feedback: The tag has the opposite sign: a positive statement takes a negative tag.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses isn't it for every sentence.

example.question: You can swim, ___?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "isn't it" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Use the helper verb of the statement and a pronoun.
misconceptions.feedback: Isn't it is not for every sentence. Use the helper verb in the statement: can, can't you.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Does not use do, does or did for a statement with no helper verb.

example.question: Otieno plays football, ___?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "isn't he" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: No helper verb? Bring in do, does or did.
misconceptions.feedback: When the sentence has only a plain verb, the tag uses do, does or did.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Writes amn't I or am not I after I am.

example.question: I am late, ___?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "amn't I" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: After I am, the tag is aren't I.
misconceptions.feedback: After I am the tag is aren't I. Amn't I is not used.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the noun again in the tag instead of a pronoun.

example.question: The girls are ready, ___?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "aren't the girls" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The tag always has a pronoun: he, she, it, they.
misconceptions.feedback: A question tag uses a pronoun (they), not the noun again.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Gives a negative tag to a negative statement.

example.question: You do not like beans, ___?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "don't you" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A negative statement takes a positive tag.
misconceptions.feedback: When the statement says not, the tag is positive: You do not like beans, do you?
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.reveals: Offer "Otieno went to the market." next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A journal is your own record, so you write I.
misconceptions.feedback: A journal is written by you about your own day, so it uses I and my.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Forgets the date at the top of an entry.

example.question: What should every journal entry begin with?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "a greeting" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Each entry is for one day, so the date comes first.
misconceptions.feedback: A journal entry begins with the date, because the entry belongs to that day.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Adds a greeting and a closing like a letter.

example.question: Which is not a part of a journal entry?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "the date" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A journal is not sent to anyone, so it has no closing.
misconceptions.feedback: A journal is private and is not sent, so it has no greeting and no Yours sincerely.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Lists only facts and leaves out feelings.

example.question: What makes a journal different from a timetable?

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "it lists the times" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: A journal is personal: it says how you felt.
misconceptions.feedback: A journal says what happened and also how you felt about it.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Pronunciation and Intensive Listening (Theme 13: Money – trade)
learning_experiences: dictate a story featuring proverbs and similes, pick them out and list them in pairs,
say the sounds: /ᴧ / as in but, / ʊ / as in put, [ ʊə] as in tour and [ eı] as in gate,
rewrite a short text in his or her own words accurately, read a written version of what they have listened to,
predict the likely outcome of events in a listening text,
pick out information such as amounts, dates, time, facts, characters, and the sequence of events from an oral text,

use expressions such as fixed phrases: at once, no entry, similes such as: sell like hot cakes, as happy as a hippo; metaphors such as - Chebet is a hare. She is so clever. proverbs such as A stitch in time saves nine, grow on trees, idioms such as back to square one, to cut corners and phrasal verbs such as count on, give in and give back.
key_inquiry_questions: Why should we listen carefully?
What is the function of similes and proverbs in communication?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Communication and Collaboration: The learner’s ability to express themselves well is enhanced as they make suggestions on improvements to be made and rewrite the short text in their own words accurately.
Creativity and Imagination: The learner’s ability to artistically communicate is developed as they rewrite the short text in own words accurately.
sub_strands.values:
Unity: This is fostered in the learner as they collaborate with peers and interact with grade-appropriate texts featuring similes and metaphors.
Integrity: This is enhanced as the learner interacts with materials on the theme of trade which enhances a sense of financial responsibility and informs them on fair trade practices.
sub_strands.pcis: Life skills (Critical Thinking): The learner develops critical thinking by predicting the likely outcome of events in a listening text.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the skill of proper pronunciation and intensive reading to the reading of texts in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify specific sounds, words, phrases, and sentences from a text
listen to a short text and rewrite it accurately
use expressions such as similes, proverbs, fixed phrases idioms and metaphors in oral contexts correctly
advocate the need for attentive listening during oral comprehension

skills.name: Use words about money and trade
skills.mastery: Chooses the right word (profit, loss, import, export, customer, retailer, wholesaler, wages, budget) for a trading situation, and does not swap the opposite pairs, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Swaps profit and loss.

example.question: Wanjiku sold the tomatoes for less than she paid. She made a ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "profit" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Profit: you get back more. Loss: you get back less.
misconceptions.feedback: Profit is the extra money you gain. Loss is money you lose when you sell for less than you paid.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Swaps import and export.

example.question: Kenya sends tea to other countries. Tea is an ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "import" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Export: out of the country. Import: into the country.
misconceptions.feedback: Exports leave the country. Imports come into the country.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Swaps retailer and wholesaler.

example.question: A ___ sells goods in small amounts to shoppers.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "wholesaler" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Retailer: sells to the public in small amounts. Wholesaler: sells large amounts to shops.
misconceptions.feedback: A retailer sells small amounts to shoppers. A wholesaler sells large amounts to shops.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Extensive Reading (Theme 13: Money – trade)
learning_experiences: skim various texts to find out the general idea,
scan a text to find specific details such as key words,
read a variety of texts of about 1251 to 1500 words from newspaper, magazines, grade-appropriate digital/print texts, as well as articles,
collaborate with peers to establish a class library,
read print and non-print materials (websites and blogs) independently,
read newspapers, magazines poems, and class readers on trade,
read digital versions of newspapers and magazines for information.
key_inquiry_questions: Why do we enjoy reading some materials but not others?
How do you obtain information from a newspaper, book, or magazine quickly?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Self-efficacy: The learner’s ability to confidently express themselves is boosted as they practise reading increasingly difficult texts.
Digital Literacy: The learner’s ability to manipulate digital devices is improved as they read online versions of newspapers.
sub_strands.values: Respect: It is fostered as the learner appreciates diverse opinions and collaborate with peers to establish a class library.
sub_strands.pcis: Financial Literacy: The learner’s knowledge on financial management is enhanced through the theme of money.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the skill of reading extensively for information to their learning in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: select appropriate reading texts from print or digital collections
read a variety of print or digital texts for enjoyment and general understanding
appreciate the importance of extensive reading in lifelong learning

sub_strands.sub_strand: Word Classes (Theme 13: Money – trade)
learning_experiences: identify prepositions of time such as since, before, until, about, during, past; directions such as above, across, below, after; agent such as by, and with; instrument such as with and by,
collaborate with peers to create visuals demonstrating the use of various prepositions,
construct sentences on money and trade using prepositions,
create crossword puzzles using prepositions in pairs or small groups,
create visuals to demonstrate the use of various prepositions in sentences,
work with peers to create charts or posters showing where objects are, for example, ‘the pupils are inside the classroom.
key_inquiry_questions: What words do we use to describe the position of people or objects in relation to others?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Learning to Learn: The learner’s ability to grasp concepts on their own is enhanced as they plan and manage time well and collaborate with peers to create and display charts featuring prepositions.
Digital Literacy: The learner’s ability to interact with digital devices is developed as they search for examples of prepositions online.
sub_strands.values:
Social Justice: It is inculcated in the learners as they display fairness while work with peers to create charts or posters showing where objects are.
Integrity: It is fostered as the learner practises accountability by constructing sentences on money and trade using prepositions.
sub_strands.pcis: Financial literacy: This is developed as the learner constructs sentences based on the theme of trade.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the skill of correct use of prepositions to their learning in Kiswahili.

outcomes.text: identify prepositions correctly in oral and written texts
use prepositions correctly in varied texts
judge the appropriateness of prepositions used in various texts

skills.name: Use between, among, since, for, during, by and the prepositions that follow words
skills.mastery: Chooses between and among, since and for, during and for, by and with, and the preposition a word takes (interested in, afraid of, different from), and does not write interested on or afraid from, in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.
Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses between for three or more, or among for two.

example.question: The sweets were shared ___ the five children.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "between" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Between: two. Among: three or more.
misconceptions.feedback: Use between for two and among for more than two.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses for with a starting point or since with a length of time.

example.question: We have lived here ___ 2019.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "for" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Since goes with a point in time; for goes with a length of time.
misconceptions.feedback: Use since with the time it began (since 2019) and for with how long (for five years).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong preposition after a word (interested on, afraid from).

example.question: Otieno is interested ___ football.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "on" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Some words take one fixed preposition: interested in, afraid of, different from.
misconceptions.feedback: Learn the pair: interested IN, afraid OF, different FROM, good AT.
misconceptions.source: Kiswahili influence (to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher)

misconceptions.error: Uses with for the doer or by for the tool.

example.question: The meat was cut ___ a knife.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "by" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: By tells who did it. With tells what was used.
misconceptions.feedback: By names the doer (by Mama). With names the tool (with a knife).
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Uses during for how long, or for for a named event.

example.question: It rained ___ the night.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "for" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: During goes with an event or a period (during the night). For goes with a number (for two hours).
misconceptions.feedback: During goes with a period such as the night or the holiday. For goes with an amount of time such as two hours.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

sub_strands.sub_strand: Mechanics of writing (Theme 13: Money – trade)
learning_experiences: identify words with prefixes and suffixes and use them to create puzzles and share with peers,
form words using prefixes and affixes,
match words with their appropriate affixes (-un, -cian, sion, - tion),
use mind maps to generate a list of related words and change their form by adding affixes,
create a crossword puzzle using the words they have generated.
key_inquiry_questions: Why is it difficult to spell some words?
How can we become better at spelling?
sub_strands.core_competences:
Self-efficacy: The learner’s ability to confidently perform tasks is developed as they show concerted attention to detail while forming words using prefixes and affixes.
Creativity and Imagination: The learner’s ability to create something new is improved as they generate ideas using mind maps and come up with a list of related words.
sub_strands.values: Peace is promoted as the learner collaborates with peers to edit and display their journals.
sub_strands.pcis: Financial Literacy: The learner is able to manage their finances better as they interact with the theme on money and trade to create mind maps and crossword puzzles.
sub_strands.links: The learner is able to relate the skill of spelling words correctly to their editing of written work in Kiswahili and other learning areas.

outcomes.text: recognise affixes used to change the form and meaning of words
form new words using prefixes and suffixes
spell words correctly for writing fluency
determine the correctness and appropriateness of affixes used in various texts

skills.name: Form new words with prefixes and suffixes
skills.mastery: Chooses the prefix (un-, dis-, mis-, re-, in-, im-) or suffix (-ful, -less, -ness, -ment, -able) that makes the meaning wanted, and keeps the spelling right (happy to happiness, care to careful), in 8 of 10 new items.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

skills.name: Spell words correctly: ie and ei, silent letters, double letters
skills.mastery: Spells words that often go wrong (receive, believe, separate, necessary, government, environment, tomorrow, library, February) from the sound, the rule or the picture of the word, in 8 of 10 new words.

prerequisites.reason: Grade 5 English taught it first. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

leads_to.reason: Grade 7 English builds on this skill. Proposed, to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher.

misconceptions.error: Uses the wrong prefix for the word (dishappy, unpossible).

example.question: ___happy

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "dis" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Each prefix goes with certain words. Say the word out loud: unhappy.
misconceptions.feedback: Each word takes its own prefix: unhappy, disagree, impossible, invisible. Learn the pairs.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Drops or adds a letter where the prefix meets the word (dissapear, mispell).

example.question: dis___appear

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "dis" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Keep every letter of both parts: dis + appear = disappear; mis + spell = misspell.
misconceptions.feedback: Keep every letter of the prefix and the word: dis + appear = disappear, mis + spell = misspell.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells the suffix -ful with two l (carefull).

example.question: care___

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "full" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: The word full is not the suffix; the suffix has one l.
misconceptions.feedback: The suffix is -ful with one l: careful, helpful.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Does not change y to i before a suffix (happyness).

example.question: happy + ness = ___

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "happyness" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: When a word ends in consonant + y, change the y to i before the suffix.
misconceptions.feedback: When a word ends in a consonant and y, change y to i before adding -ness or -ment: happiness.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Mixes ie and ei (recieve, beleive).

example.question: We ___ the parcel on Friday.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "recieved" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: I before E except after C: receive, but believe.
misconceptions.feedback: I before e, except after c: believe, but receive.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells a vowel by sound (seperate, definately).

example.question: The twins sit at ___ desks.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "seperate" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Find the word hidden inside it: sep-A-rate, like a rat.
misconceptions.feedback: Spell the vowel from the word, not from the sound: separate has an a in the middle.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Leaves out a letter that is not said (goverment, enviroment).

example.question: We must protect the ___.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "enviroment" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Say the word slowly, with every letter: environ-ment, govern-ment.
misconceptions.feedback: Some letters are not said clearly. Say it slowly: govern-ment, environ-ment.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Doubles or fails to double a letter (neccessary, tommorow, begining).

example.question: It is ___ to wash your hands before eating.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "neccessary" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: One c, one s... n-e-c-e-ss-a-r-y: one collar, two sleeves.
misconceptions.feedback: Necessary has one c and two s. Tomorrow has one m and two r.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

misconceptions.error: Spells the way it is said and loses a letter (libary, Febuary).

example.question: Our school ___ has many books.

misconceptions.cause: Common error of Kenyan learners of English.
misconceptions.reveals: Offer "libary" next to the right answer in a new sentence and ask again.
misconceptions.help: Say the r in the middle: lib-r-ary.
misconceptions.feedback: The word is library, with an r after b, and February with an r after b too.
misconceptions.source: common learner error; to confirm by a Kenyan English teacher

rubrics.heading: Suggested Assessment Rubric: Listening and Speaking

indicators.indicator: Ability to listen actively to a variety of oral texts to gain information.

levels.EE: Maintains meaningful eye-contact, sits upright, nods, takes notes, responds to oral questions correctly for information in a variety of contexts .
levels.ME: Maintains eye contact, sits upright, nods and takes notes for information in varied contexts.
levels.AE: Either maintains eye contact or sits upright or takes notes for information.
levels.BE: Yawns, looks out, has to be prompted while listening for information.

indicators.indicator: Ability to listen and participate actively in conversations in various settings for self-expression and

levels.EE: Participates actively in conversations, observes proper turn-taking skills, nods, maintains
levels.ME: Participates actively in conversations in various settings for self-expression and effective

indicators.indicator: Ability to speak accurately with expression and at the right speed, with minimum hesitation for fluency for effective communication.

levels.EE: Speaks accurately with expression and at the right speed without hesitation in varied contexts for effective communication.
levels.ME: Speaks accurately with expression and at the right speed, with minimum hesitation for fluency.
levels.AE: Speaks accurately with expression but at slow speed and with hesitation.
levels.BE: Speaks inaccurately without expression and at a slow speed with many hesitations.

indicators.indicator: Ability to read about 400 words fluently and accurately, at the right speed and with expression for effective communication.

levels.EE: Reads more than 350 words in varied texts fluently, accurately and expressively for effective communication.
levels.ME: Reads about 300 words fluently and accurately at the right speed and with expression for effective communication.
levels.AE: Reads about 800 words fluently and accurately at the right speed and with expression for effective communication.
levels.BE: Reads about 200 words fluently and accurately but at slow speed without expression.

indicators.indicator: Ability to read the text for inferential comprehension and meaning.

levels.EE: Reads a variety of texts for inferential meaning and relates to real life experiences.
levels.ME: Reads the text for inferential comprehension and meaning.
levels.AE: Reads the text for comprehension and meaning but fails to locate inferential meaning.
levels.BE: Reads the text for comprehension only.

indicators.indicator: Ability to select and read relevant materials of between 1000-1250 words for information and pleasure.

levels.EE: Selects and reads a variety of relevant materials of more than 1300 words for information and pleasure
levels.ME: Selects and reads relevant materials of between 1000-1250 words for information and pleasure.
levels.AE: Selects and reads relevant materials of below 1000 words for information and pleasure
levels.BE: Selects and reads relevant material of below 500 words and reads for information and pleasure.

indicators.indicator: Ability to write a variety of writings using the correct formats for effective communication

levels.EE: Writes a variety of writings using correct formats and uses appropriate language for varied writing tasks for effective communication
levels.ME: Writes a variety of writings using the correct formats for effective communication.
levels.AE: Writes a number of writings using correct formats for effective communication.
levels.BE: Writes all the writings using wrong formats.

indicators.indicator: Ability to plan and write compositions, coherently, clearly and logically for effective communication.

levels.EE: Plans and writes a variety of compositions coherently, clearly and logically with apt expressions and idioms for effective communication
levels.ME: Plans and writes compositions coherently, clearly and logically for effective communication
levels.AE: Plans and writes compositions with some illogical and unclear parts
levels.BE: Plans but writes compositions that are incoherent, lacks clarity and many illogical parts.
